claim: Japanese encephalitis (JE) is a mosquito-borne disease known for its high mortality and disability rate among symptomatic cases.
source: Japanese encephalitis (JE) is a mosquito-borne disease, known for its high mortality and disability rate among symptomatic cases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general characterization of JE disease.

claim: The SA 14-14-2 vaccine is recently developed and inexpensive.
source: Many effective vaccines are available for JE, and the use of a recently developed and inexpensive vaccine, SA 14-14-2, has been increasing over the recent years particularly with Gavi support.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract describing the SA 14-14-2 vaccine characteristics.

claim: In 2015, JEV infections caused 100,308 JE cases (95% CI: 61,720–157,522) globally.
source: We estimate in 2015 JEV infections caused 100,308 JE cases (95% CI: 61,720–157,522) and 25,125 deaths (95% CI: 14,550–46,031) globally
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's mathematical modeling approach using age-stratified case data.

claim: In 2015, JEV infections caused 25,125 deaths (95% CI: 14,550–46,031) globally.
source: We estimate in 2015 JEV infections caused 100,308 JE cases (95% CI: 61,720–157,522) and 25,125 deaths (95% CI: 14,550–46,031) globally
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's mathematical modeling approach.

claim: Between 2000 and 2015, 307,774 JE cases (95% CI: 167,442–509,583) were averted due to vaccination globally.
source: between 2000 and 2015 307,774 JE cases (95% CI: 167,442–509,583) were averted due to vaccination globally
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing model scenarios with and without vaccination.

claim: Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) is an arbovirus that belongs to the flavivirus genus, family flaviviridae.
source: Japanese encephalitis (JE) is caused by Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) – an arbovirus that belongs to the flavivirus genus, family flaviviridae.
evidence: This is established taxonomic classification of JEV.

claim: The main vectors of JEV are mosquitoes of the Culex genus, especially Culex tritaeniorhynchus.
source: The main vectors are mosquitoes of the Culex genus, especially Culex tritaeniorhynchus.
evidence: This is supported by cited references about JE transmission.

claim: Culex tritaeniorhynchus mosquitoes thrive in rice-paddy fields.
source: These mosquitoes thrive in rice-paddy fields (Buescher and Scherer, 1959; Self et al., 1973).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references from Buescher and Scherer, 1959 and Self et al., 1973.

claim: The amplifying hosts of JEV are thought to be pigs and wading birds.
source: JEV has a wide range of vertebrate hosts, noticeably the amplifying hosts are thought to be pigs and wading birds (SAGE Working Group on Japanese encephalitis vaccines, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited SAGE Working Group reference.

claim: Humans are dead-end hosts for JEV as viremia is not believed to reach levels that are infectious to mosquitoes.
source: Humans are dead-end hosts as viremia is not believed to reach levels that are infectious to mosquitoes (SAGE Working Group on Japanese encephalitis vaccines, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited SAGE Working Group reference.

claim: Only 1 in 25 to 1 in 1000 JEV infections result in symptoms.
source: Only 1 in 25 to 1 in 1000 infections result in symptoms (Vaughn and Hoke, 1992; SAGE Working Group on Japanese encephalitis vaccines, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references from Vaughn and Hoke, 1992 and SAGE Working Group, 2014.

claim: The mortality rate of symptomatic JE cases is around 20–30%.
source: However, the mortality rate of symptomatic cases is high - around 20–30% (Fischer et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference from Fischer et al., 2008.

claim: Around 30–50% of JE survivors experience significant neurological and psychiatric sequelae.
source: around 30–50% of survivors experience significant neurological and psychiatric sequelae (Fischer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference from Fischer et al., 2008.

claim: The first JE case was documented in Japan in 1871.
source: The ﬁrst JE case was documented in Japan in 1871 (WHO, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited WHO reference from 2015.

claim: In 1924, a first JE outbreak in Japan caused more than 6,000 cases and 3,000 deaths in 6 weeks.
source: In 1924, a first JE outbreak in Japan caused more than 6, 000 cases and 3, 000 deaths in 6 weeks (Solomon, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference from Solomon, 2006.

claim: In 2005, large JE outbreaks occurred in northern India and Nepal, with 5000 cases and 1300 deaths.
source: More recently, in 2005 large outbreaks occurred in northern India and Nepal, with 5000 cases and 1300 deaths (Solomon, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference from Solomon, 2006.

claim: Currently, 24 Asia-Pacific countries are thought to be endemic for JE.
source: Currently, 24 Asia-Paciﬁc countries are thought to be endemic for JE, with 3 billion individuals at risk of infection (WHO, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited WHO reference from 2015.

claim: 3 billion individuals are at risk of JE infection.
source: Currently, 24 Asia-Paciﬁc countries are thought to be endemic for JE, with 3 billion individuals at risk of infection (WHO, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited WHO reference from 2015.

claim: The first JE vaccine was an inactivated mouse brain vaccine produced in Japan and used worldwide for 50 years.
source: The first vaccine was an inactivated mouse brain vaccine produced in Japan, used worldwide for 50 years.
evidence: This is a historical fact about JE vaccine development.

claim: Production of the first inactivated mouse brain vaccine halted in 2006.
source: Although vaccine production halted in 2006, similar inactivated mouse brain vaccines are still produced locally in South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam (Yun and Lee, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference from Yun and Lee, 2014.

claim: Similar inactivated mouse brain vaccines are still produced locally in South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.
source: Although vaccine production halted in 2006, similar inactivated mouse brain vaccines are still produced locally in South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam (Yun and Lee, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference from Yun and Lee, 2014.

claim: The live attenuated vaccine SA 14-14-2 has been gradually replacing the inactivated Vero cell vaccine since 1988.
source: The use of the next vaccine, an inactivated a Vero cell vaccine (SAGE Working Group on Japanese encephalitis vaccines, 2014), has been gradually replaced (since 1988) by a live attenuated vaccine (SA 14-14-2) produced in China, with PATH support.
evidence: This is supported by the cited SAGE Working Group reference.

claim: SA 14-14-2 vaccine is produced in China with PATH support.
source: The use of the next vaccine, an inactivated a Vero cell vaccine (SAGE Working Group on Japanese encephalitis vaccines, 2014), has been gradually replaced (since 1988) by a live attenuated vaccine (SA 14-14-2) produced in China, with PATH support.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the SA 14-14-2 vaccine.

claim: SA 14-14-2 vaccine is now widely used in Asia and funded by Gavi.
source: SA 14-14-2 is now widely used in Asia and funded by Gavi which has led to a great increase in vaccination.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing current vaccine use.

claim: SA 14-14-2 vaccine requires only a single dose.
source: This vaccine requires only a single dose, is cheap to produce, and is safer than the mouse brain vaccine (SAGE Working Group on Japanese encephalitis vaccines, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited SAGE Working Group reference.

claim: SA 14-14-2 vaccine is cheap to produce.
source: This vaccine requires only a single dose, is cheap to produce, and is safer than the mouse brain vaccine (SAGE Working Group on Japanese encephalitis vaccines, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited SAGE Working Group reference.

claim: SA 14-14-2 vaccine is safer than the mouse brain vaccine.
source: This vaccine requires only a single dose, is cheap to produce, and is safer than the mouse brain vaccine (SAGE Working Group on Japanese encephalitis vaccines, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited SAGE Working Group reference.

claim: A live attenuated chimeric vaccine was first licensed in Australia in 2012.
source: In addition, a live attenuated chimeric vaccine was first licensed in Australia in 2012 (SAGE Working Group on Japanese encephalitis vaccines, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited SAGE Working Group reference.

claim: WHO recommends diagnosis of JE using JEV-specific IgM antibody-capture enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (MAC-ELISA) in CSF at two time points.
source: WHO recommends diagnosis using JEV-speciﬁc IgM antibody-capture enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (MAC-ELISA) in CSF at two time points (Donadeu et al., 2009; Burke and Leake, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references from Donadeu et al., 2009 and Burke and Leake, 1988.

claim: Serum samples can be used for JE diagnosis, but false positives may result from cross-reactivity with other flaviviruses or vaccination.
source: Serum samples can be used, but false positives may result from cross-reactivity with other flaviviruses or vaccination (Solomon et al., 1998; Hills et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references from Solomon et al., 1998 and Hills et al., 2009.

claim: The previous estimate of annual global JE cases was 67,900 with 13,600–20,400 deaths.
source: The previous estimate of annual global JE cases was 67,900 with 13,600–20,400 deaths (Campbell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference from Campbell et al., 2011.

claim: A systematic review on October 11th 2017 yielded 2337 initial results.
source: A systematic review on October 11th 2017 yielded 2337 initial results (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a methodological finding from the systematic review process, also shown in Figure 2.

claim: 407 relevant studies were obtained after eliminating 1931 irrelevant titles and abstracts.
source: 407 relevant studies were obtained after eliminating 1931 irrelevant titles and abstracts that were about molecular biology, policy, entomology, hosts other than humans, or were review papers.
evidence: This is a methodological finding from the systematic review process.

claim: 261 full-text papers were retrieved and read.
source: We retrieved and read 261 full-text papers.
evidence: This is a methodological finding from the systematic review process.

claim: 53 studies contained age-stratified case data.
source: Finally, we had 53 studies that contained age-stratified case data (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a methodological finding from the systematic review process, also shown in Figure 2.

claim: 42 of the 53 studies (79%) contained data from after 2000 only.
source: 42 of the 53 studies (79%) contained data from after 2000 only, 7 from before 2000 only and three from both time periods (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding about the temporal distribution of the studies included.

claim: 34 studies (64%) had data from 1 to 4 year time periods.
source: 34 studies (64%) had data from 1 to 4 year time periods, six studies had data for periods of between 5 and 9 years, and 11 studies had data for more than 10 years.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding about the temporal coverage of the studies included.

claim: FOI estimates varied from 0.001 (95% CI: 0.000 - 0.002) in Japan to 0.507 (95% CI 0.419 - 0.582) in Guigang in China.
source: Our FOI estimates varied from 0.001 (95% CI: 0.000 - 0.002) in Japan to 0.507 (95% CI 0.419 - 0.582) in Guigang in China.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the catalytic model fitting to age-stratified case data.

claim: FOI were generally between 0.05 and 0.2, with a median of 0.09.
source: Besides those extreme values, FOI were generally between 0.05 and 0.2, with a median of 0.09 (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary finding from the FOI estimates, also shown in Figure 4.

claim: From 2000 to 2015, there were 1,976,238 (95% CIs: 1,722,533–2,725,647) JE cases globally.
source: We estimate that from 2000 to 2015, there were 1,976,238 (95% CIs: 1,722,533–2,725,647) JE cases globally.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the burden estimation model.

claim: Had there been no vaccination from 2000 to 2015, there would have been 2,284,012 (95% CIs: 1,495,964–3,102,542) JE cases.
source: By including known annual vaccination information in the catalytic model we estimate that in the same period had there been no vaccination there would have been 2,284,012 (95% CIs: 1,495,964–3,102,542) JE cases.
evidence: This is a counterfactual estimate from the burden estimation model comparing scenarios with and without vaccination.

claim: Vaccination programs prevented 74,769 deaths from JE (95% CIs: 37,837–129,028) from 2000 to 2015.
source: vaccination programs similarly prevented 74,769 deaths from JE (95% CIs: 37,837–129,028).
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing model scenarios with and without vaccination.

claim: The greatest impact of vaccination was from 2005 to 2010 due to large increase in vaccination in China in this time.
source: We estimate the greatest impact of vaccination from 2005 to 2010 due to large increase in vaccination in China in this time, and the impact of vaccination became more obvious over time (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference from the burden estimation model results, also shown in Figure 5.

claim: In 2015, vaccination reduced the number of cases globally by around 45,000 (from 145,542 (95% CI: 96,667–195,639) to 100,308 (95% CI: 61,720–157,522)).
source: In 2015, we estimate vaccination reduced the number of cases globally by around 45,000 (from 145,542 (95% CI: 96,667–195,639) to 100,308 (95% CI: 61,720–157,522) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing model scenarios with and without vaccination, also shown in Figure 5.

claim: The highest number of cases was estimated in the high endemic area of China (around 40,000 annual cases in the no vaccination scenario and around 20,000 annual cases in vaccination scenario).
source: We estimated the highest number of cases in the high endemic area of China (around 40,000 annual cases in the no vaccination scenario and around 20,000 annual cases in vaccination scenario)
evidence: This is a finding from the burden estimation model for specific regions.

claim: Medium or high endemic areas in India had around 20,000 annual cases in no vaccination scenario and 15,000 annual cases in vaccination scenario for each area in recent years.
source: and medium or high endemic areas in India (around 20,000 annual cases in no vaccination scenario and 15,000 annual cases in vaccination scenario for each area in recent years).
evidence: This is a finding from the burden estimation model for specific regions.

claim: Areas like Australia, Brunei, Bhutan and Russia were estimated to have less than 100 annual cases with or without vaccination.
source: On the contrary, areas like Australia, Brunei, Bhutan and Russia were estimated to have less than 100 annual cases with or without vaccination (Figure 5, Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the burden estimation model for specific regions, also shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: In the high endemic area in China, routine vaccination programs only started in 2008 but contributed the most to the global cases reduction, with around 20,000 cases averted in China in 2015.
source: Indeed, in the high endemic area in China, the routine vaccination programs only started in 2008 but contributed the most to the global cases reduction, with around 20,000 cases averted in China in 2015.
evidence: This is a finding from the burden estimation model comparing scenarios with and without vaccination.

claim: A clear difference in cases between vaccination and no vaccination scenario was observed in areas with intensive vaccination programs such as South Korea, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Taiwan, and Vietnam.
source: We also observed a clear difference in cases between vaccination and no vaccination scenario in areas with intensive vaccination programs such as South Korea, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Taiwan, and Vietnam.
evidence: This is a finding from the burden estimation model comparing scenarios with and without vaccination.

claim: For Japan, Australia, and Malaysia, though vaccination began a long time ago, minimal vaccine impact was estimated.
source: For Japan, Australia, and Malaysia, though vaccination began a long time ago, we estimated there has been minimal vaccine impact.
evidence: This is a finding from the burden estimation model comparing scenarios with and without vaccination.

claim: No vaccine programs had occurred in Bangladesh, Brunei, Bhutan, the low and high endemic areas in Indonesia, Myanmar, Pakistan, Philippines, Papua New Guinea, Russia, or Singapore.
source: From the data we collated, no vaccine programs had occurred in in Bangladesh, Brunei, Bhutan, the low and high endemic areas in Indonesia, Myanmar, Pakistan, Philippines, Papua New Guinea, Russia, or Singapore so we estimated of course vaccination has had no impact.
evidence: This is based on the vaccination data collated from literature review, WHO, and Gavi.

claim: The global estimate of around 100,000 cases annually is about 1.5 times higher than the previous estimate of around 70,000 cases.
source: Our global estimate of around 100,000 cases annually is about 1.5 times higher than the previous estimate of around 70,000 cases (Campbell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current study's findings with previous estimates from Campbell et al., 2011.

claim: The high FOI estimated in the south of China, Vietnam, and Philippines is consistent with the high pig density and high probability of Culex in these areas.
source: The high FOI estimated in the south of China, Vietnam, and Philippines is consistent with the high pig density and high probability of Culex in these areas (for Vietnam and Philippines with Miller et al., 2012 only).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing FOI estimates with environmental covariates from cited references.

claim: High FOI was estimated in India and Indonesia; however these countries only have high probability of Culex but low pig density.
source: We also estimated high FOI in India and Indonesia; however these countries only have high probability of Culex (in Miller et al., 2012 but not Longbottom et al.) but low pig density in Longbottom et al., 2017.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing FOI estimates with environmental covariates from cited references.

claim: Other potential animal reservoirs may contribute to JE transmission in India and Indonesia, likely the wading bird or even poultry.
source: This suggests that other potential animal reservoirs may contribute to the transmission in these countries, likely the wading bird or even poultry, although current evidence is limited (Lord et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the discrepancy between FOI estimates and known environmental factors, with limited evidence cited.

claim: In Taiwan and South Korea the current estimated FOI is lower compared to other areas, respectively 0.061 (95% CI 0.013–0.093), and 0.041 (95% CI 0.026–0.057).
source: In Taiwan and South Korea the current estimated FOI is lower compared to other areas, respectively 0.061 (95% CI 0.013–0.093), and 0.041 (95% CI 0.026–0.057)
evidence: This is a finding from the FOI estimation model.

claim: Urbanization, which reduces the proximity of humans to pig farms and rice fields, may play an important role in lowering JE transmission.
source: This could be due to lack of recent data, or perhaps suggests urbanization, which reduces the proximity of humans to pig farms and rice fields (where the mosquitoes thrive), may play an important role in lowering transmission.
evidence: This is a speculative inference to explain the lower FOI in Taiwan and South Korea.

claim: For China and Japan, lower susceptible proportions after vaccination in certain age groups were estimated compared to calculated proportions from the available data.
source: For China and Japan we estimated lower susceptible proportions after vaccination in certain age groups compared to calculated proportions from the available data.
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian model fitting comparing posterior estimates with prior vaccination data.

claim: The lower susceptible proportions in China and Japan suggest that there are a large number of immunized people in certain age groups due to past vaccination, for which information was not available.
source: This suggests that there are a large number of immunized people in certain age groups due to past vaccination, for which we did not have information.
evidence: This is an inference from the discrepancy between model estimates and available vaccination data.

claim: From 2006 to 2011, SA 14-14-2 vaccine was used in India for campaigns.
source: From 2006 to 2011, SA 14-14-2 vaccine was used in India for campaigns.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about vaccination programs in India.

claim: SA 14-14-2 vaccine reported nearly 100% efficacy in vaccine trials and case-control studies.
source: Though the vaccine reported nearly 100% efficacy in vaccine trials and case-control studies (Kumar et al., 2009; Bista et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by the cited references from Kumar et al., 2009 and Bista et al., 2001.

claim: The efficacy of SA 14-14-2 vaccine in India was reported to be as low as 30% to 40%.
source: the efficacy in India was reported to be as low as 30% to 40% (Vashishtha and Ramachandran, 2015; Tandale et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by the cited references from Vashishtha and Ramachandran, 2015 and Tandale et al., 2018.

claim: Lower seroconversion has been reported in India for SA 14-14-2 vaccine.
source: and lower seroconversion has also been reported in India (Singh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference from Singh et al., 2015.

claim: A previous evaluation showed that the vaccination coverage data in India was lower than reported.
source: A previous evaluation of vaccination coverage also showed that the vaccination coverage data in India was lower than reported (Murhekar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference from Murhekar et al., 2017.

claim: Cross-reactive immunity to other flaviviruses could be a possible explanation for different vaccine efficacies in different places.
source: One possible explanation could be cross-reactive immunity to other flaviviruses, or differences in circulating JE genotypes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observed differences in vaccine efficacy.

claim: Differences in circulating JE genotypes could be a possible explanation for different vaccine efficacies in different places.
source: One possible explanation could be cross-reactive immunity to other flaviviruses, or differences in circulating JE genotypes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observed differences in vaccine efficacy.

claim: The burden estimates are highest in China and India by region.
source: By region, our burdens estimates are highest in China and India, which aligns with previous literature (Heffelfinger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the burden estimation model, consistent with previous literature.

claim: The method more robustly takes into account under-reporting and different surveillance quality compared to previous estimates.
source: It is not surprising that our estimates are higher, since our method more robustly takes into account under-reporting and different surveillance quality.
evidence: This is an explanation for why the current estimates are higher than previous estimates, based on methodological improvements.

claim: The estimates include population changes and the progression of vaccination programs over time.
source: In addition, the numbers we reported here are time-dependent and not static because our estimates include population changes and the progression of vaccination programs over time.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The estimate of vaccination impact will be an underestimate of the total impact because the impact of vaccination will continue into the future as vaccinated individuals remain protected.
source: Because the impact of vaccination will continue into the future as vaccinated individuals remain protected, our estimate will be an underestimate of the total impact of vaccination.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the scope of the vaccination impact estimates.

claim: The estimates will be an under-estimate of total vaccine impact as in some places vaccination programs have been running before 2000.
source: In addition, our estimates will be an under-estimate of total vaccine impact as in some places vaccination programs have been running before 2000, and so vaccination had a large impact before 2000.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the temporal scope of the vaccination impact estimates.

claim: A large number of JE cases have long-term sequelae after infection.
source: However because a large number of cases have long-term sequelae after JE infection, focus just on case numbers does not describe fully the total burden of JE.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about JE disease outcomes.

claim: JE vaccination does not produce herd immunity.
source: Since JE vaccination does not produce herd immunity, the transmission intensity can only be reduced by influencing the animal transmission cycle.
evidence: This is based on the understanding that humans are dead-end hosts for JEV.

claim: Previous attempts to break the JE transmission cycle have been vector control and vaccination in pigs and wading birds.
source: Previous attempts to break the transmission cycle have been vector control and vaccination in pigs and wading birds, and this has been considered in modelling work (Khan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference from Khan et al., 2014.

claim: Previous attempts to break the JE transmission cycle were either ineffective or have been deemed economically and logistically intensive.
source: However they were either ineffective or up to now have been deemed economically and logistically intensive (Fischer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference from Fischer et al., 2008.

claim: Human vaccination can be an effective strategy to reduce JE case numbers despite not interrupting transmission.
source: We estimate that despite not interrupting transmission, human vaccination can be an effective strategy to reduce JE case numbers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the vaccination impact estimates.

claim: The majority of the reduction in global burden is due to the routine vaccination program in China from 2008.
source: This can be seen from the estimate that the majority of the reduction in global burden is due to the routine vaccination program in China from 2008.
evidence: This is a finding from the burden estimation model comparing scenarios with and without vaccination.

claim: India, Timor-Leste, and Vietnam have high transmission intensity and residual cases despite vaccination, and could further benefit from scaling-up the existing vaccination program.
source: We estimate that India, Timor-Leste, and Vietnam also have high transmission intensity, and residual cases despite vaccination, and therefore could further benefit from scaling-up the existing vaccination program (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the FOI estimates and burden estimates from the model.

claim: High transmission intensity was estimated in Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, and Philippines where there are no current vaccination programs, suggesting that vaccination in these areas should be a future priority.
source: We estimated high transmission intensity in Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, and Philippines where there are no current vaccination programs, suggesting that vaccination in these areas should be a future priority.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the FOI estimates and absence of vaccination programs.

claim: A substantial vaccine impact was estimated in South Korea, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Taiwan with a long history of JE vaccination.
source: For areas with a long history of JE vaccination (see Figure 3—source data 1). such as South Korea, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Taiwan, (Figure 4), we estimate a substantial vaccine impact (Figure 5), though with cases still occurring.
evidence: This is a finding from the burden estimation model comparing scenarios with and without vaccination.

claim: Minimal impact of vaccination was estimated in Japan, Malaysia, and Australia despite long vaccination history.
source: In other countries with a long vaccination history however, we estimate a minimal impact of vaccination (Figures 4 and 5), due to low estimated transmission intensity in Japan, low vaccination coverage in Malaysia, or both in Australia
evidence: This is a finding from the burden estimation model with explanations for the minimal impact.

claim: There are limitations to how well the method will work in Japan given the high rate of vaccination there.
source: In addition, there are limitations to how well our method will work, given the high rate of vaccination there.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a methodological limitation for areas with high vaccination coverage.

claim: The study may be under-estimating the impact of vaccination in Japan.
source: This may mean we are under-estimating the impact of vaccination in Japan.
evidence: This is an inference about a potential limitation in the estimates for Japan.

claim: Annually there are still 100,000 cases of JE in Asia.
source: We estimate annually there are still 100,000 cases of JE in Asia
evidence: This is a primary finding from the burden estimation model for 2015.

claim: 2/3 of all JE cases are still not being averted despite vaccination being available.
source: making a 2/3 of all cases of this severe but vaccine preventable still not being averted.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the number of cases with and without vaccination scenarios.

claim: The majority of remaining JE cases are focused in countries with still developing healthcare systems.
source: The majority of remaining cases are focussed in countries with still developing healthcare systems.
evidence: This is an inference based on the geographic distribution of estimated cases.

claim: The systematic review used search terms 'epidemiology' or 'incidence' or 'prevalence' or 'public health' or 'surveillance' or 'distribution' in all fields with 'Japanese encephalitis' in the title or abstract.
source: We used the search terms 'epidemiology' or 'incidence' or 'prevalence' or 'public health' or 'surveillance' or 'distribution' in all fields with 'Japanese encephalitis' in the title or abstract.
evidence: This is a description of the systematic review methodology.

claim: Vaccination information was obtained from three main sources: literature review, WHO, and Gavi.
source: We obtained the vaccination information from three main sources: literature review, WHO, and Gavi (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a description of the data sources for vaccination information.

claim: Campaign vaccination information was mainly from Gavi and routine vaccination was from WHO.
source: Campaign vaccination information was mainly from Gavi and routine vaccination was from WHO, while the literature contains both.
evidence: This is a description of the data sources for different types of vaccination information.

claim: When there were disagreements between different vaccination information sources, information from the literature review was used.
source: When there were disagreements between the different vaccination information sources, we chose to use the information from the literature review.
evidence: This is a description of the decision rule for handling conflicting vaccination data.

claim: The study assumed that the JE vaccine has 100% effectiveness.
source: We assumed that the JE vaccine has 100% effectiveness, which is reasonable given the reported high effectiveness of the vaccine (World Health Organization, 2012a; WHO, 2014; World Health Organization, 2012b)
evidence: This is a methodological assumption supported by cited references about vaccine effectiveness.

claim: The study assumed that protection acquired from natural infection or vaccination was life-long.
source: and that the protection acquired from natural infection or vaccination was life-long.
evidence: This is a methodological assumption about immunity duration.

claim: The endemic areas were defined to be the same as in the previous JE burden estimate by Campbell et al., 2011.
source: For our estimate, the endemic areas were defined to be the same as in the previous JE burden estimate (Campbell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a methodological decision to use the same geographic classification as previous work.

claim: For China, India, Nepal and Indonesia, where transmission intensity is diverse, these countries were broken down to low, medium, or high endemic areas.
source: For China, India, Nepal and Indonesia, where transmission intensity is diverse these countries were broken down to low, medium, or high endemic areas.
evidence: This is a methodological decision about geographic stratification.

claim: In total, there are 30 endemic areas, spanning 24 countries.
source: In total, there are 30 endemic areas, spanning 24 countries.
evidence: This is a summary of the geographic scope of the study.
